title: How to work satin stitch in cross-stitch
subtitle: Parallel straight stitches for smooth filled areas
excerpt: Satin stitch fills a shape with parallel straight stitches packed tightly side by side. It appears in cross-stitch pieces as a smooth contrast to the textured cross-stitch fill, most often in floral petals and leaves. The challenge is keeping the edges neat and the stitches parallel.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, embroidery chapter. Satin stitch is one of the most documented filling stitches in Victorian needlework literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: A filling technique using parallel straight stitches laid side by side across a shape until the fabric is completely covered. The stitches should lie exactly parallel and touch without overlapping. The resulting surface appears smooth and slightly raised, with a sheen similar to satin fabric.

content.text: fills a shape with parallel straight stitches, each running from one side of the shape to the other. In cross-stitch pieces, satin stitch appears as a smooth contrast element alongside the
, most commonly in floral or decorative work where one area needs a different texture.
It is not a counted stitch: satin stitch does not follow the Aida grid holes precisely. The outline of the satin stitch area is often marked by a
first, giving the shape a clean edge to work up to.

Work a back-stitch outline around the area to be filled with satin stitch. The outline gives you a precise edge to meet with each straight stitch and prevents the fill from spreading beyond the design boundary.
Work the first stitch across the widest point.
Find the widest part of the shape and work the first stitch from one edge to the other. This establishes the angle of all subsequent stitches.
Work stitches outward from the centre stitch.

Place each new stitch immediately beside the previous one, parallel and touching. Work to one side of the centre stitch, then return and work the other side. The stitches should cover the outline thread where they meet it.
Pull each stitch to the same tension as the one before it. Uneven tension makes the surface look corrugated rather than smooth.

Two strands give a good coverage for most shapes. Three strands give a more raised, bolder satin stitch suitable for larger areas. Silk thread produces an especially smooth finish if the pattern calls for it; standard DMC cotton floss is the default.
